I completely disagree with Michael Burry’s view on Palantir. Burry has bought $100 put options expiring in March 2027 and argues that the stock is ultimately worth less than $1. His reasons include the high valuation multiple, the size of stock-based compensation, and off-balance-sheet commitments. These are important issues, but they don’t reflect the company’s current reality. Palantir’s latest quarterly results are clear: revenue grew 93%, U.S. commercial revenue increased 149%, profit margins reached the 55–62% range, and the company significantly raised its full-year guidance. These numbers don’t point to a “bubble”; they demonstrate real demand and strong operational execution. The fact that the commercial business is growing rapidly and approaching the scale of the government business proves that Palantir is not simply a defense software company. A high valuation always carries risk. But when a company has strong growth, high profitability, and solid net cash generation, arguing that it is worth “less than $1” is extreme and unrealistic. As long as growth continues, these valuation multiples can become more reasonable over time. Burry’s thesis seems to be stuck on past accounting concerns while overlooking the company’s current momentum. In short: Palantir’s business model is working, and the results support that. I disagree with Burry’s extremely bearish view. $PLTR

$ARM Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM) — Short Thesis ~$282 | Trailing P/E 288x | Forward P/E 118x | EV/EBITDA 261x | EV/FCF 198x | PEG 3.33 1. The multiple is priced for growth the business no longer delivers Q1 FY27 revenue grew 22% to $1.29B. That is a good business — it is not a 288x business. The semiconductor industry median forward P/E is 30x; Arm sits 328% above it, ranking 503rd of 552 peers. Worse, the trend is against it: management cut full-year royalty growth guidance to the high teens from 20%, and guided Q2 royalty growth to just 13%. A 3.33 PEG on decelerating royalties is the entire setup. 2. Operating leverage is running backwards GAAP operating margin fell to 7.1% from 10.8% as operating expenses rose 28% against 22% revenue growth. For a licensor with 98% gross margins, that is the wrong direction. Non-GAAP operating margin “improved” to 41.2% — the entire narrative lives in the adjustment. GAAP TTM EPS is $0.97 against a $282 stock. 3. The AGI CPU pivot buys revenue with margin Arm is moving from licensing IP to selling silicon. Management guides first-gen AGI CPU gross margins to high-30s/low-40s in FY27–28, with a path toward 50% over time. Against ~98% blended today. The $25B FY31 revenue target is real, but the market is capitalizing it at IP-licensor economics that will not exist at $25B. Mix shift is the bear case, not the bull case. 4. Channel conflict with its own royalty base Selling chips puts Arm in competition with the licensees who fund it — Qualcomm, MediaTek, and hyperscalers building custom Neoverse silicon. Those same customers already bankroll RISC-V as negotiating leverage. Arm is monetizing near-term at the cost of long-term pricing power. 5. The core remains levered to a shrinking end market Royalties are still majority smartphone. Memory-driven price inflation is now hitting mid-tier and premium handsets, not just the low end management initially expected. Data center royalties more than doubled — genuinely strong, but off a base too small to carry the model alone. Structure Beta 3.91. The stock fell 34% in July on a sector-wide semi selloff, then reclaimed $280 within days. SoftBank’s controlling stake leaves a thin float. This is not a size-up-and-hold short. What kills the thesis The AGI CPU is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained: demand tops $2B against $1B in secured supply. If Arm lands capacity and data center royalties keep doubling, the growth reaccelerates before the margin dilution bites. The balance sheet is fortress-grade — $3.9B cash, $665M quarterly free cash flow — so there is no solvency or refinancing catalyst. That leaves you with a pure valuation short, which requires a market-wide multiple reset to work, and that timing is unknowable. Note also that the last print beat at the top of guidance and the stock still fell 8% — expectations may already be resetting without you.

$HPE The price is above all the 20/50/100/200 EMAs, with a perfect alignment: 49.93 > 46.12 > 40.51 > 33.99. It has once again reached the top of the sideways range that has been in place for the past two months. If we get a daily close above 55.31, the next targets are 59.11 → 64.09 → 78.60. The fundamentals are telling the same story. Revenue grew 40% last quarter, EPS doubled, the AI backlog reached $5.9 billion, and free cash flow guidance was raised from $2 billion to $3.5 billion. Juniper synergies are also running ahead of schedule. Despite all of this, the stock is trading at just 16x earnings. Morgan Stanley upgraded it to Overweight yesterday, with a $69 price target. If the range breaks out, there’s very little resistance above.

$LLY Q2’26 revenue came in at $23B, up 48% YoY. Mounjaro + Zepbound alone generated $14.9B. Gross margin was 86.3%. Full-year guidance was raised to $85–87B. Foundayo has just entered the market, the Medicare program has opened access to 20 million people at $50/month, and retatrutide is heading to the FDA in Q1 2027. The story is still in its early stages. Technically, the price is above all the 20/50/100/200 EMAs, with the moving averages properly aligned. The channel that started in May remains intact, and MACD has crossed above zero to the upside. If $1,240 breaks, the upside looks wide open. Growth is accelerating, margins are expanding, and there isn’t a single sign of technical deterioration on the chart.

$ASTS – My View After Q2 2026 Earnings This quarter confirmed that ASTS is still in the infrastructure build-out phase. Revenue grew strongly, guidance was maintained, and liquidity improved materially. The main negative is that commercial subscriber revenue is still ahead, so execution remains the key risk. Revenue was $31.5M, roughly double sequentially but below the ~$34–35M expected. Revenue is still coming from gateway equipment and government milestones, meaning direct-to-device monetization is largely a 2027 story. Net loss was $230.9M, mainly due to the ~$125.9M impairment from the BB7 loss. Capex was $610M, reflecting heavy manufacturing and launch spending. The strongest part of the quarter was liquidity. Cash was $2.7B at June 30 and exceeded $3.7B pro forma after the July convertible offering. With limited effective dilution and a low coupon, I view the financing positively. Backlog also increased to $1.3B. The key question now is how quickly cash burn accelerates as deployment scales. On the call, ASTS highlighted 13 satellites in orbit, BB14–16 nearing shipment and production progressing through BB46. The target remains six satellites per month, with roughly 45 satellites expected to support commercial service by early 2027. Beta service is expected to begin with selected operators in 2026. The $1B first-full-commercial-year revenue target remains intact, with potentially up to half coming from government business. Japan’s J-LEO opportunity could also provide up to $1B of non-dilutive capital. The stock fell roughly 4.4% after earnings. To me, this looked more like an expectations-vs-results reaction than a fundamentally bad quarter. Guidance and liquidity remained strong. Bull case: A direct-to-device network connecting to unmodified phones addresses a potentially massive market. The operator model, spectrum, technology and vertical integration could create a strong competitive position. Government business could provide both capital and recurring revenue. Bear case: Execution remains the biggest risk. Launch delays, manufacturing scale-up, network performance, high capex and commercialization timing are all critical. Pricing, subscriber economics and churn are still unproven. What I’m watching: satellite launches, beta performance, government contracts, cash burn, commercial rollout, operator economics and satellite production costs. Bottom line: My long-term thesis has not changed and, if anything, strengthened slightly. The thesis remains: build the constellation, monetize through mobile operators, and use government business to reduce risk. I expect volatility, but I would need to see a meaningful execution failure to materially change my view.

Baird upgraded $FSLR to Outperform, with a $318 price target (up from $205). Key reasons: • Strong utility-scale solar market • Resolution of Section 232 uncertainty • Better-calibrated estimates and greater clarity on capital allocation A resolution of the Section 232 issue could restart 2029–2030 bookings, potentially at higher ASPs.
